items.prompt: What does owning a share of stock represent?

options.label: A deposit held at a bank for safekeeping
A loan made to a company that it repays
A partial ownership stake in a company
A guaranteed yearly payment from a company

rubric: A share is a slice of company ownership.
Loans to a company describe bonds, not stocks.

items.prompt: What is a bond?

options.label: A share of ownership in a company's profits
A basket that holds only company shares
A loan you make to a government or company in exchange for interest
A savings account insured by the government

rubric: A bond is a loan paid back with interest.
Ownership describes stock, not bonds.

items.prompt: What does diversification mean in investing?

options.label: Putting all money into your best idea
Moving money in and out of the market often
Spreading money across different investments
Buying only investments from one country

rubric: Diversification spreads money across many holdings.
Concentrating in one idea is the opposite.

items.prompt: What is an expense ratio on a fund?

options.label: The yearly fee charged as a percentage of assets
The profit the fund earned last year
The share of the fund held in stocks
The minimum amount needed to buy the fund

rubric: Expense ratio is the annual fund fee as a percent of assets.
Other options describe return, allocation or minimum purchase.

items.prompt: What is an index fund?

options.label: A fund that aims to match a market index
A fund that holds only cash and savings
A fund guaranteed never to lose value
A fund that tries to beat the market by picking winners

rubric: Index funds track a market index.
Beating the market describes active funds.

items.prompt: Which of the following are common asset classes for investors? Select all that apply.

options.label: Stocks
Monthly rent bills
Credit card balances
Cash equivalents
Bonds

rubric: Stocks, bonds and cash equivalents are core asset classes.
Debts and bills are not investment assets.

items.prompt: Maya just opened an investing account. A friend says, "Your portfolio is the full collection of everything you hold in your accounts." Maya holds a stock fund, a bond fund and some cash. What does the term portfolio refer to?

options.label: All her investments taken together
Only the stock fund she bought first
The app she uses to buy investments
The fees she pays for each purchase

rubric: A portfolio is the total collection of holdings.
Distractors confuse it with one holding, a tool or a cost.

items.prompt: Why do stocks usually offer higher expected returns than savings accounts over long periods?

options.label: Stock prices are set by the government
Banks refuse to pay interest on savings
Investors are paid for accepting more risk of loss
Stocks are guaranteed to rise every year

rubric: Higher expected return compensates for higher risk.
Stocks have no guarantee of yearly gains.

items.prompt: Why does holding many different stocks reduce risk compared with holding one?

options.label: Fees fall to zero when you own many stocks
Losses are refunded when you own more than ten
Every stock in the group rises at the same time
One company's bad result affects only a small part of the total

rubric: Spreading limits the damage from any one failure.
Stocks do not all move together, and diversification does not remove fees or refund losses.

items.prompt: A fund charges 1.0% a year and another similar fund charges 0.1%. Why does this gap matter over decades?

options.label: Fees are taken once at purchase and then stop
Higher fees always buy better investment results
Fees only matter in years when the fund loses money
Fees reduce returns every year and the loss compounds

rubric: Annual fees drag on returns and compound over time.
Fees are charged regardless of performance and do not ensure better results.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains the relationship between risk and return?

options.label: Higher potential returns usually come with higher chance of loss
Risk and return are unrelated to each other
Return is guaranteed once risk is understood
Low-risk investments typically give the highest returns

rubric: Risk and potential return tend to rise together.
Understanding risk does not guarantee returns.

items.prompt: Which of these portfolios is the best example of a diversified one?

options.label: A fund holding stocks from many companies plus a bond fund
All savings in one company's stock bought at work
Only the single stock that rose most last year
Shares of three companies in the same industry

rubric: Diversification spans many companies and asset types.
Same-industry or single holdings keep risk concentrated.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe why a bond fund is usually less volatile than a stock fund? Select all that apply.

options.label: Bond prices never change at all
Bonds typically pay set interest on a schedule
Bond funds are guaranteed by the government
Bond holders are generally repaid before stock owners if a company fails

rubric: Fixed interest and repayment priority make bonds steadier.
Bond prices do change and funds are not guaranteed.

items.prompt: Leo is 25 and sees his stock fund drop 15% in a month. He plans to use the money in 30 years. A friend urges him to sell everything now. Which explanation best describes why selling may hurt him?

options.label: It guarantees he pays no fees on future purchases
It turns the loss into a gain at tax time
It protects him because markets never recover
It locks in the loss and he misses the recovery over his long horizon

rubric: Selling after a drop locks in losses and can miss rebounds for long-term goals.
Selling does not erase losses, and markets have historically recovered.

items.prompt: Which risk does spreading money across many different companies and sectors mainly reduce?

options.label: The risk that a fund company raises its fees
The risk that prices rise across the whole economy
The risk that the entire stock market falls together
The risk that one company or sector performs badly

rubric: Diversification cuts company- or sector-specific risk because one holding's failure is offset by others.
Market-wide falls and inflation affect all holdings, so diversifying stocks alone does not remove them.

items.prompt: Why do high-quality bonds usually swing less in value than stocks?

options.label: Bond buyers become part owners, so they share in profits and vote on company decisions
Bond issuers promise set interest and repayment of principal, while share prices depend on uncertain profits
Bond prices are set once a year, while share prices are reset daily by the stock exchange
Bonds are insured by the government against any loss, while shares carry no protection at all

rubric: Bonds are loans with contractual payments, giving steadier values than ownership shares.
Distractors confuse bonds with insured deposits or with ownership.

items.prompt: What does a fund's expense ratio of 0.40% tell you?

options.label: You pay a 0.40% fee once, when you first buy
The fund holds 0.40% of its money in cash
Each year 0.40% of your invested amount goes to fund costs
The fund has earned 0.40% in profit each year

rubric: The expense ratio is an annual percentage of assets deducted to run the fund.
Distractors treat it as a return, a one-time charge or a cash holding.

items.prompt: What is an index fund?

options.label: A fund whose manager picks a few stocks expected to beat the market
A fund that guarantees a minimum return set by a stock index
A fund that holds the securities in a market index to match its performance
A fund that only holds bonds issued by large governments

rubric: Index funds passively mirror an index's holdings and results.
Distractors describe active management, bond funds or guaranteed products.

items.prompt: When market interest rates rise, what usually happens to the price of an existing bond paying a lower fixed rate?

options.label: It rises, because buyers want older bonds
It rises, because the bond now looks safer
It stays the same, because the payments are fixed
It falls, because new bonds pay more and buyers want a discount

rubric: Older lower-rate bonds must sell at a discount to compete with new higher-rate bonds.
Fixed payments do not mean a fixed price before maturity.

items.prompt: Which statements about risk and return are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Combining different asset types can lower swings in a portfolio's value
Stock returns are guaranteed to be positive over any ten-year period
Assets with higher expected returns generally come with greater chance of losses
Holding only cash has no risk because balances never fall in nominal terms

rubric: Higher expected return usually means higher risk, and mixing assets smooths volatility.
Stocks have no guarantee over ten years, and cash still loses purchasing power to inflation.

items.prompt: Maya works for a tech company and keeps 80% of her savings in its stock because she believes in it. A colleague says this is risky even if the company is doing well. Which explanation best captures the colleague's point?

options.label: Company stock pays no dividends, so it cannot grow her savings over time
Owning a single stock is illegal beyond a certain share of savings
A problem at the company could cut her pay and her savings together, with little else to offset it
Company stock always falls when employees own too much of it

rubric: Concentration links job income and savings to one company, which is a specific, avoidable risk.
Distractors invent rules or false claims about stock behaviour.

items.prompt: You hold $10,000 in a fund with a 0.50% expense ratio. About how much do you pay in fees over one year, ignoring growth?
rubric: Other options come from misplacing the decimal point.

items.prompt: Your target is 60% stocks and 40% bonds. After a rally you hold $7,000 in stocks and $3,000 in bonds. What restores the target?

options.label: Sell $3,000 of stocks and buy $3,000 of bonds
Keep everything, since the stocks are winning
Sell $1,000 of bonds and buy $1,000 of stocks
Sell $1,000 of stocks and buy $1,000 of bonds

rubric: Total is $10,000, so 60% is $6,000 in stocks; move $1,000 from stocks to bonds.
Other choices move the wrong direction, overshoot or skip rebalancing.

items.prompt: A rule of thumb says stock percentage equals 100 minus your age. Using it, how much should a 35-year-old hold in stocks?
rubric: 100 - 35 = 65% in stocks.
Other options use age directly or misapply the subtraction.

items.prompt: Two funds track the same broad stock index. Fund A charges 0.05% a year; Fund B charges 0.80%. You want the better long-run result. Which do you pick?

options.label: Fund A, because the holdings are the same and lower fees leave more return
Fund B, because it will hold different stocks than the index
Fund B, because a higher fee signals better management
Fund A, because lower fees mean the fund is guaranteed to beat the index

rubric: Same index means similar gross returns, so the lower fee gives a higher net return.
Distractors assume price signals quality or that low fees guarantee outperformance.

items.prompt: You buy 10 shares at $50, later sell them at $60, and received $5 total in dividends. What is your total return on the $500 invested?
rubric: 20% leaves out the dividends, and the others slip on the percentage calculation.

items.prompt: A new investor with a 20-year horizon wants a simple diversified plan. Which actions fit that plan? Select all that apply.

options.label: Put everything into last year's best-performing stock
Set automatic monthly contributions
Sell all holdings whenever the market drops 5%
Buy a broad total-market stock fund and a bond fund

rubric: Broad funds plus regular contributions follow a simple diversified, long-term approach.
Chasing winners concentrates risk, and selling on small dips locks in losses.

items.prompt: Sam invests $100 each month in an index fund. The share price is $20 in month one, $10 in month two and $25 in month three. Fractional shares are allowed. How many shares does Sam own after three months?
rubric: Other answers come from averaging prices or miscalculating one month.

items.prompt: A portfolio is targeted at 70% stocks and 30% bonds. After a strong year, a $100,000 portfolio holds $80,000 in stocks and $20,000 in bonds. To rebalance back to target using only existing money, what should you do?

options.label: Sell $20,000 of stocks and buy $20,000 of bonds
Keep holdings and wait for bonds to catch up
Sell $10,000 of stocks and buy $10,000 of bonds
Sell $10,000 of bonds and buy $10,000 of stocks

rubric: Target stocks is $70,000 and bonds $30,000, so move $10,000 from stocks to bonds.
Selling $20,000 overshoots the target; selling bonds deepens the drift.

items.prompt: An index fund returns 7% per year before fees and charges a 1.0% expense ratio. Assuming a constant return, about what is the annual return after the fee?
rubric: Net return is about 7% minus 1% = 6%.
The 6.9% option treats the fee as 1% of the return rather than 1% of assets.

items.prompt: You invest $500 every month into the same fund. The price per share is $50 in month one, $25 in month two, and $50 in month three. How many shares do you own after three months?

options.label: 30 shares
33 shares
60 shares
40 shares

rubric: 10 + 20 + 10 = 40 shares, so average cost is $37.50.
Averaging the prices ($41.67) gives about 36 shares, and other options ignore that more shares are bought when prices are low.

items.prompt: You hold a 10-year bond fund with an average duration of about 7 years. Interest rates rise by 1 percentage point. Using duration as a rule of thumb, what is the approximate change in the fund's price?

options.label: Fall of about 70%
Fall of about 1%
Fall of about 7%
Rise of about 7%

rubric: Price change is roughly negative duration times the rate change: -7 x 1% = -7%.
Rising rates push bond prices down, not up; confusing years with percent inflates the figure.

items.prompt: A stock position is 40% of a $50,000 portfolio. You want no single holding above 10%, and you sell down to the limit. How much of that stock do you sell?
rubric: Position is $20,000; a 10% limit is $5,000; sell $15,000 (ignoring changes in total value).
Selling $5,000 or $10,000 mistakes the limit amount for the amount to sell.

items.prompt: You are building a simple diversified portfolio for a 25-year goal using broad index funds. Which steps follow sensible procedure? Select all that apply.

options.label: Rebalance back to target when allocations drift beyond a set band
Choose low-expense-ratio funds that cover many companies
Move into last year's top-performing fund each January
Set a stock and bond allocation based on your time horizon and risk tolerance

rubric: Allocation, low-cost broad funds and rule-based rebalancing are the standard procedure.
Chasing last year's winner is performance chasing and not part of the procedure.

items.prompt: Maya, 30, has a $12,000 emergency fund, no high-interest debt, and $400 spare each month. Her employer offers a 401(k) with a 50% match up to 6% of her $60,000 salary, and she contributes nothing yet. What is the best next step?

options.label: Contribute at least 6% to capture the full match, investing in a diversified fund
Contribute 1% for now to avoid tying up money
Keep saving the $400 in cash until she has a year of expenses saved
Buy individual stocks in a taxable account to grow faster

rubric: A 50% match is an immediate 50% return on those contributions, and her emergency fund and debt are already handled.
Waiting or contributing 1% forfeits matching money.

items.prompt: Two funds each average 8% a year over 20 years. Fund A has annual swings of about 10%. Fund B has annual swings of about 25%. What does this comparison mainly show?

options.label: Fund B carried more risk for the same average return, so it was less efficient
Fund A must hold more bonds, because only bonds have lower swings
Fund B must have the higher long-run growth because of its larger swings
The two funds are equivalent, since average return is all that matters

rubric: Same return with higher volatility means worse risk-adjusted performance.
Volatility does not guarantee higher return, and low volatility has other possible causes.

items.prompt: An investor owns five funds: a US large-cap index fund, an S&P 500 ETF, a total US market fund, a US growth fund and a dividend fund. She thinks she is highly diversified. What is the most accurate analysis?

options.label: She is well diversified because each fund has a different provider and name
She is under-diversified only because she lacks individual stocks
She is diversified because five is enough funds to remove market risk
Holdings overlap heavily in the same US large companies, so diversification is much lower than five funds suggest

rubric: Funds that hold the same large US companies move together, so fund count overstates diversification.
Fund names and counts do not remove shared exposure or market risk.

items.prompt: Over 15 years a fund beat the market by 1% per year before fees, yet the investor's account lagged a plain index fund. The fund charges 1.4% in expenses and 0.3% in trading costs versus 0.05% for the index fund. What best explains the lag?

options.label: The fund's extra return was taxed more than the index fund's gain
Past outperformance guarantees later underperformance
Costs of about 1.65% a year exceeded the 1% edge, leaving a net shortfall
The index fund took more risk, which always pays off

rubric: Net edge is about 1% minus 1.6% extra cost, around -0.6% a year, compounding over time.
Risk does not always pay off, taxes are not mentioned, and no rule makes outperformance reverse.

items.prompt: A 60/40 stock/bond portfolio fell 18% in a year when both stocks and bonds dropped, as interest rates rose sharply. Which diagnosis fits best?

options.label: Diversification never works and the portfolio should be all stocks
Rebalancing caused the losses by selling winners
The bonds must have defaulted
Stock-bond diversification weakened because rate rises hurt both asset classes at once

rubric: Rising rates cut bond prices while pressuring stock valuations, so their usual offset failed.
Price falls do not mean default, and diversification still helps over many conditions.

items.prompt: Investor X and Investor Y both earned a fund's 9% annual return over 10 years. X invested $10,000 at the start. Y invested $1,000 each year for 10 years. Why did X end with much more money?

options.label: X's full amount compounded for the whole period, while most of Y's contributions had fewer years to grow
X took less risk by investing at once
Y paid higher fees because of the smaller deposits
Y earned a lower rate of return because deposits were spread out

rubric: Equal totals invested, but time in the market differs; earlier dollars compound longer.
The fund return was the same, and lump-sum investing does not lower risk.

items.prompt: A saver in her 50s holds 95% stocks in one sector fund and plans to retire in 5 years. Which are valid problems in this setup? Select all that apply.

options.label: Concentration in one sector adds risk that broad diversification would reduce
Sequence risk: early losses near retirement can permanently damage withdrawals
Holding stocks always guarantees losses over five years
A short horizon leaves little time to recover from a major drawdown

rubric: Sector concentration, short recovery time and sequence risk all raise the danger.
Stocks do not guarantee losses over any period; they are volatile.

items.prompt: Leo checks his portfolio, which is 80% in a global stock index fund and 20% in a bond fund. Stocks fell 25% in six months. He sold all stocks, intending to buy back once things 'feel safe'. Six months later, stocks have risen 30%. Which analysis best explains why his plan hurt his results?

options.label: The bond fund must have underperformed, which caused his shortfall
Global index funds cannot recover from falls of this size
He locked in the loss and missed the rebound, since recoveries often begin before conditions feel safe
Selling stocks reduced his fees, which hurt returns

rubric: Market timing based on feelings often misses early rebounds, turning paper losses into real ones.
Fees and the bond fund are not the cause, and diversified indexes have historically recovered.

items.prompt: Two funds track the same broad stock index over ten years. Fund X returned 7.1% a year and Fund Y returned 6.2% a year. Which explanation best accounts for the gap?

options.label: Fund Y charged higher fees and trading costs, which are subtracted from the same underlying return every year
Fund Y held riskier stocks, which always earn less than the stocks held by Fund X
Fund X had more holdings, and a larger number of holdings raises the return of an index
Fund X was timed better by its manager, who moved to cash before each market decline

rubric: Funds tracking the same index earn the same gross return, so the gap is mostly costs.
Distractors treat risk or manager timing as a driver, but index trackers do not time the market.

items.prompt: In a year when interest rates rose sharply, a 60/40 stock/bond portfolio fell in value on both sides, and diversification offered little cushion. What best explains this?

options.label: The bond portion was too small, because any bond share above 40% prevents losses
Rising rates cut existing bond prices while also lowering stock valuations, so both fell together
Bonds and stocks are always positively correlated, so mixing them never lowers risk
Diversification only works inside one asset class, never across stocks and bonds

rubric: A common driver, rising rates, hit both asset classes at once, so correlation rose.
Distractors overgeneralise: stocks and bonds are not always correlated, and allocation size alone cannot prevent losses.

items.prompt: An investor holds three funds: an S&P 500 index fund, a total US stock market fund and a large-cap growth fund. She believes this is well diversified. What is the most accurate analysis?

options.label: It is balanced, because the growth fund offsets the risk in the two index funds
It is under-diversified, because all three funds hold mostly the same large US companies and move together
It is over-diversified, because holding more than two funds lowers expected return below the market
It is well diversified, because three separate funds from different providers always means three independent risks

rubric: The funds overlap heavily in large US stocks, so the number of funds overstates diversification.
Distractors confuse the number of funds with the number of distinct risk exposures.

items.prompt: A investor set a 70% stock / 30% bond target. After a long rally her portfolio is 82% stock / 18% bond and she has done nothing. What does this drift mean for her portfolio?

options.label: It is unchanged in risk, because her contributions alone decide how risky a portfolio is
It is now diversified more widely, because the stock part has grown to be larger
It carries less risk than before, because winning assets in a portfolio lower overall volatility
It carries more risk than she chose, because the stock share has grown beyond the target and raises possible losses

rubric: Drift raises the stock weight, so volatility and drawdown exposure exceed the intended level.
Distractors treat gains as risk-reducing or diversifying.

items.prompt: A bond fund has an average duration of 7 years. Market interest rates rise by 1 percentage point. Which outcome is most consistent with this?

options.label: The fund's price rises about 7%, since higher rates mean higher yields on the bonds
The fund's price falls roughly 7%, though higher yields on new holdings later offset some of this
The fund's price falls roughly 1%, since rates moved by one point
The fund's price stays flat, because bond funds hold bonds until maturity

rubric: Duration approximates percentage price change per one-point rate move, so about -7%, with later income recovering some loss.
Distractors ignore duration or assume bond funds are immune to price changes.

items.prompt: An investor wants to pick the fund with the best five-year record from a list of 400 funds. Which factors make that record an unreliable guide to future results? Select all that apply.

options.label: With so many funds, some will rank first through luck alone rather than skill
Funds that closed after poor results are dropped from lists, so the surviving records look better
Five-year records are unreliable only for funds with fees above 2%
Strong results often came from a style that was favoured in that period and may fall out of favour

rubric: Survivorship bias, luck among many funds and style-regime dependence all weaken the link between past and future returns.
The fee-threshold option is false: these problems apply regardless of fee level.

items.prompt: A 35-year-old put all her house deposit savings into a global stock index fund. She needs the money in two years. The fund then fell 25%, and she must now delay her purchase. She blames the fund for being poor. What is the best diagnosis of what went wrong?

options.label: The fund was badly chosen, since a global index fund is too volatile for any investor
The fund should have been sold before the fall, because a sensible investor can see declines coming
The fund was fine, but a two-year need clashes with stocks' short-term swings, so the asset did not suit the time horizon
The deposit should have been spread over more stock funds, since that removes market-wide drops

rubric: The cause is a mismatch between a short horizon and a volatile asset, not the fund itself.
Distractors blame the fund, assume timing is feasible, or think more stock funds remove market risk.

items.prompt: A long-term saver compares a broad index fund (0.05% annual fee) with an actively managed fund (0.90% fee) with the same holdings style. Her criteria are: maximise expected net return over 30 years and avoid relying on finding a skilled manager in advance. Which choice best fits?

options.label: The index fund, because the fee gap compounds over 30 years and outperformance cannot be known in advance
The active fund, because a manager can limit losses in every falling market
Either fund, because a fee under 1% a year makes no real difference over 30 years
The active fund, because paying more reliably buys higher returns over three decades

rubric: Low fees compound in the investor's favour and the criteria rule out depending on picking a winner.
Distractors assume cost buys performance or that small fees do not compound.

items.prompt: An investor receives a lump sum of 60,000 and has a 20-year horizon. Her criteria: maximise expected long-run value and she can tolerate short-term losses. She considers investing it all now or spreading it over 12 months. Which is the best judgement?

options.label: Hold it in cash until prices fall, because a drop is certain before the next rise
Spread it over 12 months, because that guarantees a lower average purchase price
Spread it over 12 months, because this raises expected return by avoiding all down periods
Invest it all now, because markets rise more often than not, so waiting tends to cost expected return, though it risks short-term regret

rubric: Given her stated criteria, lump-sum investing has the higher expected value; phasing in mainly reduces regret.
Distractors claim phasing raises return or guarantees a lower price, or encourage waiting for a drop.

items.prompt: A retiree is about to start withdrawing from a portfolio of stocks and bonds. Criterion: rank the risk most likely to permanently damage how long the money lasts. Which ranks highest?

options.label: Missing a year of high returns later in retirement, when the balance is small
Large stock losses in the first years of withdrawals, since selling at low prices locks in the damage
Holding too few funds, since three funds cannot spread risk
A fund's expense ratio changing by 0.02% in a given year

rubric: Sequence-of-returns risk is greatest early in withdrawals because selling in a downturn shrinks the base permanently.
Distractors name risks with far smaller effects on how long the money lasts.

items.prompt: After a 12% market drop, an investor sells all his stock funds, planning to return "when things look clearer." Which critique is strongest?

options.label: His plan is sound if he returns within a year, since a year is long enough for any recovery
His only error is selling every fund, since selling half would have guaranteed a good outcome
His plan needs two correct calls, when to exit and when to re-enter, and the best recovery days often come close to the worst
He is right to sell, because avoiding further drops always beats staying invested

rubric: Timing needs two right decisions, and large rebounds cluster near large drops, so sitting out often costs more than it saves.
Distractors assume exits are reliably profitable or that a partial sale guarantees success.

items.prompt: An employee has 40% of her investments in her employer's stock. Criteria: keep the loss of income and savings from a single company's failure low, and avoid unnecessary tax or fee drag. Which action best fits?

options.label: Keep the holding, since she knows the company better than outside investors do
Move the whole 40% into a single rival company, so the sector view is unchanged
Buy more shares, since loyalty to the employer tends to be rewarded with higher returns
Gradually sell down the stock into a broad low-cost index fund, because her pay and savings share one company's fate

rubric: Her job and her savings are exposed to the same firm, so reducing concentration into a broad fund addresses the criteria.
Distractors rely on familiarity or swap one concentrated bet for another.

items.prompt: A saver proposes holding 100% of her stock allocation in companies from her home country. Which are sound criticisms of this plan, judged by the aim of reducing risk without lowering expected return? Select all that apply.

options.label: It is flawed because home-country stocks are legally barred from long-term holding
It ignores that other markets hold many large companies whose returns do not move in step with hers
It leaves her exposed to one economy, one currency and one market's long slumps
It is guaranteed to have lower returns than any foreign market

rubric: Single-country concentration adds risk that international holdings can reduce without a known cost to expected return.
The other options state falsehoods: there is no such bar and no guaranteed return ranking.

items.prompt: An investor wants a hands-off approach. In the last downturn he sold half his funds at a loss and later regretted it. He is choosing between a three-fund portfolio of his own at 0.06% a year and a target-date index fund at 0.12% that rebalances automatically. His criteria are low cost and limiting the chance he will tinker. Which option is the best judgement?

options.label: The target-date fund, because the small extra fee buys automatic rebalancing and fewer decisions at which he might panic
A concentrated fund of one hot sector, because it should recover its losses quickly
The three-fund portfolio, because the lower fee outweighs any behaviour concerns in every case
Cash held outside the market, because it removes the need for any decisions

rubric: His history shows behaviour is the main risk, so a slightly pricier automatic option fits both criteria.
Distractors ignore the behaviour criterion, chase a hot sector, or avoid investing altogether.

items.prompt: An investor holds five funds: an S&P 500 index fund, a US large-cap growth fund, a US dividend-growth fund, a US technology sector fund and a total US market fund. Judged against the goal of real diversification, which critique is best?

options.label: The funds have different names but heavily overlapping US large-cap holdings, so returns will be highly correlated
Five funds is too few, since meaningful risk reduction only starts once a portfolio holds at least thirty funds
The overlap is harmless, because each fund charges a different fee and the fee differences offset the correlation
Mixing growth, dividend and sector funds balances income against growth and so removes most equity market risk

rubric: The funds largely hold the same US large-cap companies, so the number of funds overstates diversification.
Distractors confuse fund count or style labels with low correlation.

items.prompt: An advisor says a 0.75% higher annual fee is trivial. A $10,000 lump sum grows 30 years at 7% gross in a low-fee fund, or 6.25% net in the pricier fund, with no other flows. Which evaluation of the claim is most accurate?

options.label: Negligible, because a 0.75% gap is small next to a 7% return and averages out across different market cycles
About 8% lower, because fees apply only to the gains and the gains in early years are small relative to the base
About 22% lower, because 0.75% a year over 30 years adds up in a straight line to roughly 22.5% of the end value
About 19% lower, because the fee cuts the growth rate itself, so each year's lost return also stops compounding

rubric: (1.0625/1.07)^30 is about 0.81, so the ending value is roughly 19% lower.
Distractors use simple linear addition or dismiss fee drag as noise.

items.prompt: Two investors receive the same set of annual returns over 30 years, including one severe crash. Investor X has the crash in year 1, Investor Y in year 30. Compare the effect on a retiree withdrawing 4% of the starting balance each year. Which statement is best supported?

options.label: The crash hurts most a saver making monthly contributions early on, because those contributions cannot recover from falling prices
With ongoing withdrawals an early crash leaves a smaller base to recover, so the retiree ends lower; with no flows the order is irrelevant
Order never matters for either investor, because identical annual returns always give an identical average return and ending balance
Order matters little for a retiree, because withdrawals are a fixed share and shrink automatically when the balance falls

rubric: Sequence-of-returns risk arises only when cash flows occur; a lump sum's ending value is order-independent.
Distractors ignore cash flows or reverse the effect for accumulators, who actually buy cheaply after early crashes.

items.prompt: A taxable account holds a 70/30 stock/bond target. Each trade has a spread cost and sales trigger capital gains tax. Drift rarely exceeds 3 points in a year, and the owner adds money monthly. Criteria: keep risk near target, minimise tax and trading cost. Which policy is best?

options.label: Rebalance each quarter by selling winners to the exact target, because calendar discipline matters more than tax or cost
Steer new contributions to the underweight asset and sell only if drift passes a set band such as 5 points
Sell and reset to exactly 70/30 every month, so risk never strays from the target and discipline is never in doubt
Never rebalance and let winners run, because selling winners always triggers taxes that exceed any benefit from risk control

rubric: Contribution-based rebalancing with tolerance bands controls risk while avoiding most taxable sales and costs.
Distractors over-trade or abandon risk control entirely.

items.prompt: A parent needs $60,000 for tuition due in exactly 7 years and wants the bond money's value then to be as certain as possible, whichever way interest rates move. Which holding best meets this criterion?

options.label: A high-quality bond fund or ladder with duration near 7 years, because price and reinvestment effects offset at that point
A 3-month Treasury bill fund, because tiny price swings mean the value at year 7 is fixed regardless of rate changes
A 20-year Treasury fund, because its higher yield will outweigh price falls if rates rise before year 7
A high-yield corporate bond fund, because the extra income cushions price changes whichever way rates move

rubric: Matching duration to the horizon immunises against parallel rate shifts.
Distractors ignore reinvestment risk (bills), or take on too much rate or credit risk.

items.prompt: A marketer shows a backtest in which a rule-based momentum strategy beat a broad stock index by 3% a year over 20 years. Which are valid grounds to doubt you would earn that result? Select all that apply.

options.label: A strategy that beat an index once is bound to keep doing so, so doubt about the result is unnecessary
Trading costs and taxes from high turnover may not have been subtracted from the reported returns
The rules may have been tuned after seeing the data, so results reflect fitting to that specific past period
The test may include only companies still listed today, leaving out failed firms and inflating past returns
Twenty years is long enough that any outperformance must be pure luck, so the result is meaningless

rubric: Survivorship bias, ignored costs and data-mining are standard backtest flaws.
The other options claim luck is certain or persistence is guaranteed; neither follows.

items.prompt: Dana, 45, has 40% of her net worth in her employer's stock, bought long ago at a low cost basis, so sales would trigger large gains. Her salary and bonus also depend on the company. She wants lower risk but dislikes a large tax bill in a single year. Which plan best fits her criteria?

options.label: Sell some and buy shares of the company's main competitors, because the same industry knowledge hedges the risk
Hold all of it, since the large gains mean tax on a sale is costly and she already knows the company well
Sell it all this year into a diversified fund, since concentration risk outweighs any tax bill however large it is
Sell in stages over several tax years, put proceeds into broad index funds and use any losses to offset the gains

rubric: Her job and wealth are tied to one firm; staged sales cut idiosyncratic risk while spreading the tax cost as she asked.
Distractors ignore either the concentration risk or her stated tax preference, or swap in sector concentration.

items.prompt: A 65-year-old retiree with $1M spends $40,000 a year and needs the money to last 30 years. The design must (1) avoid selling stocks after big declines to fund spending and (2) keep enough growth for 30 years. Which design meets both?

options.label: Hold 2 to 3 years of spending in cash and short bonds, the rest in diversified stocks and bonds, refilling the cash after good years
Hold 100% stock index funds and sell shares monthly, because long-run growth means short declines do not matter much
Hold only high-dividend stocks and spend the dividends alone, since the shares then never need to be sold in a decline
Move everything to bonds and cash, because that removes any need to sell stocks and keeps spending money safe

rubric: A spending buffer avoids forced stock sales in downturns while the rest stays invested for growth.
Distractors satisfy only one constraint, or rely on dividends that can be cut and concentrate sectors.

items.prompt: An investment policy statement specifies 70% global stock index funds, 30% aggregate bond fund, funds costing under 0.2% a year, and monthly contributions. What is the most important element it is missing to work through a severe market crash?

options.label: A sleeve of individual stocks chosen for upside, so that the portfolio has a chance of beating the index in a crash
A forecast of next year's market return, so that the stock and bond weights can be reset to match the outlook
A pre-committed rule for rebalancing bands and for staying invested during drawdowns, written before a crash occurs
A stop-loss order on each fund at a 10% decline, so that losses are capped before they grow into larger ones

rubric: Allocation and costs are set, but behaviour rules during drawdowns and drift are absent.
Distractors add timing, stop-losses that lock in losses, or stock-picking that adds risk.

items.prompt: An investor has $200,000 in a taxable account and $200,000 in a tax-deferred 401(k). The goal is an overall 60% global stock index / 40% bond fund mix while minimising annual tax drag. Which placement meets every constraint?

options.label: Put all stock funds in the 401(k) and all bonds in the taxable account, since stocks have higher growth to shelter
Hold 60/40 inside each account, so that each account is balanced on its own and rebalancing is simple
Put the $160,000 bond fund in the 401(k) with $40,000 of stocks, and the other $200,000 of stock index in taxable
Hold bonds in the taxable account for liquidity, and keep stocks in the 401(k) where their growth is deferred

rubric: Bond interest is taxed at ordinary rates, so bonds go in the tax-deferred account; the overall mix remains 60/40.
Distractors ignore tax-efficient location or fail to reach the overall target.

items.prompt: A euro-based retiree wants the bond portion of her portfolio to dampen overall volatility and keep spending power in euros. Which bond design best meets this stability constraint?

options.label: Global aggregate bonds hedged back to euros, since removing currency swings stops them adding equity-like volatility
Hedged bonds paired with unhedged stocks only, since hedging both would remove all return from the portfolio
Emerging-market local-currency bonds, since their higher yields compensate for currency moves and stabilise returns
Unhedged global bonds, since holding many currencies spreads the risk and the swings will cancel out over time

rubric: Currency moves can be as volatile as stocks, so hedged bonds serve the stabiliser role for euro liabilities.
Distractors treat currency exposure as free diversification or yield as stability.

items.prompt: Two 35-year-olds have equal savings and goals. One is a tenured government employee, the other earns commission at a stock brokerage. To keep total risk, including future income, similar for both, which design is right?

options.label: The broker holds more stock, since a higher income lets him absorb losses and keep investing through crashes
The broker holds a lower stock share, since his income already moves with markets, while the employee can hold more
Both hold identical allocations, since age, savings and goals alone should determine a sensible asset mix
The broker concentrates in finance stocks, since his industry knowledge gives him an edge in picking winners

rubric: Future income is a bond-like or stock-like asset; commission pay tied to markets calls for less equity in the portfolio.
Distractors ignore income correlation or double down on it.

items.prompt: A couple, 38, needs an $80,000 house down payment in 3 years and also saves for retirement in 27 years. They want low fees and little effort. Which design elements meet all the constraints? Select all that apply.

options.label: Keep the down-payment money in short-term Treasuries or insured deposits, separate from the retirement investments
Invest retirement savings in a low-cost diversified stock and bond index mix suited to a 27-year horizon
Put the down payment in a stock index fund, since 3 years is long enough to ride out declines reliably
Pick a few individual growth stocks for both goals, since faster growth shortens the time needed to save
Put both goals in one 2055 target-date fund, since a single fund keeps things simple for every goal

rubric: Each goal needs an asset mix matching its horizon: safe for the 3-year goal, growth for the 27-year one.
Distractors apply equity risk to the short-term goal or treat different horizons as one.

items.prompt: Priya inherits $200,000 and targets an 80/20 stock/bond index mix. She would be tormented if she invested everything just before a drop, but does not want to time the market or leave cash idle indefinitely. Which plan fits all her constraints?

options.label: Invest equal tranches monthly over about six months into the 80/20 mix, on a schedule fixed in advance regardless of news
Hold cash until a 10% market pullback appears, then invest it all at once at the lower prices
Hold bonds for a year first, then switch to stocks once the market feels calmer and less likely to fall
Invest everything at once immediately, since expected value favours it and her feelings should not influence the plan

rubric: A pre-set, time-limited phased schedule limits regret, avoids timing calls and ends with full investment.
Distractors rely on timing, ignore her stated tolerance, or delay indefinitely.
